title_options: Why Rain Doubles Your Braking Distance 🌧️
facts: UK Highway Code rule 227: in wet weather stopping distances will be at least double those required on dry roads, because tyres have less grip; rule 231: in snow and ice braking distances can be ten times greater.
Braking distance d = v^2 / (2a); braking deceleration is limited by tyre grip, so half the grip -> twice the distance. Worked: 50 km/h, dry 7 m/s^2 -> ~14 m; wet 3.5 m/s^2 -> ~28 m.
Tyre tread grooves channel water out from under the tyre; worn tyres clear less water.
description: On a wet road your car needs at least twice as far to stop. Here's why, with two cars braking side by side. #shorts #physics #science #cars
sources: UK Highway Code rules 227 and 231 (gov.uk); braking distance = speed^2 / (2 x deceleration) (GCSE physics).

scenes.narration: On a wet road, your car can need at least twice as far to stop.
Both of these cars brake at fifty kilometres an hour. One on a dry road, one on a wet road.
The dry car stops in about fourteen metres. The wet one slides on to about twenty-eight.
Braking works by grip between the tyre and the road, and water gets in between and cuts that grip.
Half the grip means half the braking force, so the same speed takes twice the distance.
Worn tyres make it worse, because their grooves can't push the water away.
So how much farther do you think a car needs on ice?
